payload.title: Permanganate titration of iron in an ore

stimulus.description: A student dissolves a $0.800\text{ g}$ sample of iron ore in acid so that all of the iron is present as Fe²⁺ and dilutes the solution to $100.00\text{ mL}$. A $25.00\text{ mL}$ portion is titrated with $0.0250\text{ M}$ KMnO₄. The balanced equation is MnO₄⁻ + 5 Fe²⁺ + 8 H⁺ → Mn²⁺ + 5 Fe³⁺ + 4 H₂O. The endpoint is reached after $18.40\text{ mL}$ of KMnO₄ has been added.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Calculate the number of moles of MnO₄⁻ added at the endpoint and the number of moles of Fe²⁺ in the $25.00\text{ mL}$ portion.

rubric_rows.criterion: Calculates the moles of MnO₄⁻ (about 4.600e-04 mol)
common_errors: uses the volume in mL without converting to liters

rubric_rows.criterion: Multiplies by 5 for the moles of Fe²⁺ (about 2.300e-03 mol)
common_errors: uses a 1:1 mole ratio

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Calculate the mass percent of iron in the ore sample.
parts.model_answer: The 100.00 mL solution holds 4 × 2.300e-03 = 9.200e-03 mol Fe, which is 0.5138 g; mass percent = 0.5138/0.800 × 100 = 64.2%.

rubric_rows.criterion: Scales the moles of Fe²⁺ from the 25.00 mL portion to the 100.00 mL solution (about 9.200e-03 mol)
common_errors: uses only the moles in the 25.00 mL portion

rubric_rows.criterion: Converts to the mass of iron and divides by the ore mass (about 64.2%)
common_errors: divides by the mass of the portion instead of the whole sample

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: No indicator was added to the flask. Explain how the student can still identify the endpoint.
parts.model_answer: MnO₄⁻ is purple and is reduced to nearly colorless Mn²⁺ while Fe²⁺ remains; once all of the Fe²⁺ has reacted, the first excess drop of MnO₄⁻ leaves a faint persistent pink color.

rubric_rows.criterion: States that the endpoint is the first persistent pink or purple color
common_errors: says the solution becomes colorless at the endpoint

rubric_rows.criterion: Justifies that MnO₄⁻ is consumed (reduced to colorless Mn²⁺) until the Fe²⁺ is gone, so the excess MnO₄⁻ colors the solution
common_errors: says Fe²⁺ itself produces the pink color

parts.label: D
parts.prompt: A bubble was trapped in the tip of the buret before the titration and left the tip during the titration. Will the calculated mass percent of iron be too high, too low, or unaffected? Justify your answer.
parts.model_answer: Too high: the bubble volume is counted as titrant delivered, so the recorded volume is larger than the volume that reacted.

rubric_rows.criterion: States that the mass percent of iron will be too high
common_errors: says it will be too low

rubric_rows.criterion: Justifies that the buret reading overstates the volume of KMnO₄ that reacted, which overstates the moles of Fe²⁺
common_errors: says the concentration of KMnO₄ changes

parts.label: E
parts.prompt: Identify the oxidizing agent in the reaction and justify your answer using oxidation numbers.
parts.model_answer: MnO₄⁻ is the oxidizing agent: the oxidation number of Mn decreases from +7 to +2, so MnO₄⁻ is reduced and oxidizes Fe²⁺.

rubric_rows.criterion: Identifies MnO₄⁻ as the oxidizing agent
common_errors: identifies Fe²⁺ as the oxidizing agent

rubric_rows.criterion: Cites the change in the oxidation number of Mn from +7 to +2, showing that it is reduced
common_errors: uses the oxidation number of iron without noting that it increases

payload.title: Electrolysis of copper sulfate solution

stimulus.description: A student electrolyzes $1.0\text{ M}$ CuSO₄(aq) between two inert electrodes, using a constant current of $2.50\text{ A}$ for $20\text{ minutes}$. Copper metal forms on one electrode, and a gas forms on the other. Use F = 96,485 C/mol e⁻.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Calculate the total charge, in coulombs, and the number of moles of electrons that flow.

rubric_rows.criterion: Calculates the charge (3000 C) using the time in seconds
common_errors: uses the time in minutes

rubric_rows.criterion: Divides by the Faraday constant (about 0.0311 mol e⁻)
common_errors: multiplies by the Faraday constant

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Calculate the mass of copper that forms.
parts.model_answer: Cu²⁺ + 2 e⁻ → Cu, so n(Cu) = 0.0311/2 = 0.0155 mol and the mass is 0.99 g.

rubric_rows.criterion: Uses two moles of electrons per mole of Cu (about 0.0155 mol Cu)
common_errors: assumes one mole of electrons per mole of Cu

rubric_rows.criterion: Converts to the mass of copper (about 0.99 g)
common_errors: omits the molar mass

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: The gas formed at the other electrode is O₂, from 2 H₂O → O₂ + 4 H⁺ + 4 e⁻. Calculate the volume of O₂ at 298 K and 1.00 atm.

rubric_rows.criterion: Uses four moles of electrons per mole of O₂ (about 0.00777 mol)
common_errors: uses two moles of electrons per mole of O₂

rubric_rows.criterion: Applies PV = nRT for about 0.190 L
common_errors: uses the temperature in °C

parts.label: D
parts.prompt: Identify the electrode at which copper forms and justify your answer.
parts.model_answer: Copper forms at the cathode: Cu²⁺ gains electrons and is reduced, and reduction occurs at the cathode.

rubric_rows.criterion: Identifies the electrode at which copper forms as the cathode
common_errors: identifies the anode

rubric_rows.criterion: Justifies with Cu²⁺ gaining electrons (reduction), which occurs at the cathode
common_errors: says oxidation occurs at the cathode

parts.label: E
parts.prompt: The student repeats the electrolysis with the current doubled. Predict the time needed to deposit the same mass of copper and justify your answer.
parts.model_answer: Half as long: the same mass requires the same charge, q = It, so doubling the current halves the time.

rubric_rows.criterion: States that the time needed is half as long
common_errors: says the time stays the same

rubric_rows.criterion: Justifies that the same mass needs the same total charge and q = It
common_errors: says the mass depends only on the current

payload.title: Method of initial rates and the rate law

stimulus.description: Initial rates for A + B → products at one temperature

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Determine the order of the reaction with respect to A and with respect to B. Justify each answer with the data.
parts.model_answer: Doubling [A] with [B] fixed multiplies the rate by 2, so the order in A is 1; doubling [B] with [A] fixed multiplies the rate by 2, so the order in B is 1.

rubric_rows.criterion: Finds the order 1 in A by comparing experiments 1 and 2 (rate ratio 2)
common_errors: compares experiments in which both concentrations change

rubric_rows.criterion: Finds the order 1 in B by comparing experiments 1 and 3 (rate ratio 2)
common_errors: uses the coefficient from the equation

rubric_rows.criterion: Relates each rate ratio to the factor by which the concentration changed
common_errors: gives the orders without using the data

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Write the rate law for the reaction and calculate the value of the rate constant, including units.

rubric_rows.criterion: Writes rate = k[A]^1[B]^1
common_errors: includes a product or a concentration with the wrong exponent

rubric_rows.criterion: Calculates k (about 0.0125 M⁻¹ s⁻¹) with units
common_errors: omits the units of k

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Calculate the initial rate when [A]₀ = 0.15 M and [B]₀ = 0.3 M.

rubric_rows.criterion: Substitutes the concentrations into the rate law
common_errors: uses the concentrations of experiment 1

rubric_rows.criterion: Calculates the rate (about 5.625e-04 M/s)
common_errors: adds the terms instead of multiplying

parts.label: D
parts.prompt: The temperature is increased and the experiments are repeated. The rate constant increases. Explain this increase in terms of the molecules that react.
parts.model_answer: A larger fraction of collisions has energy at least equal to the activation energy at the higher temperature, so more collisions are effective and the rate constant is larger.

rubric_rows.criterion: States that a larger fraction of collisions has enough energy to react
common_errors: says the activation energy decreases

rubric_rows.criterion: Connects the energy to the activation energy at the higher temperature
common_errors: says the concentration of the reactants increases

parts.label: E
parts.prompt: A student proposes that the reaction occurs in a single elementary step A + B → products. Is the proposal consistent with the rate law? Justify your answer.
parts.model_answer: Consistent: for a single elementary step the rate law would be rate = k[A][B], which matches the experimental rate law.

rubric_rows.criterion: States that the proposal is consistent because an elementary step has orders equal to its coefficients, rate = k[A][B]
common_errors: decides from the coefficient of the overall equation without considering the experimental orders
